newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks set 6th straight record, dollar mixed.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks set 6th straight record, dollar mixed.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks rose to a sixth straight record Wednesday as Wall Street welcomed the Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged.
The dollar rose against the Japanese yen but fell to a 49-month low against the British pound. Oil and gold rose. Bond prices edged lower.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 8.20 points to 6,274.24, surpassing Tuesday's record finish of 6,266.04.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,289 to 1,109 on moderate volume of 429 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks also set a new high, with a gain of 0.73 point to 386.91.

The Dow has risen nearly 250 points over the past seven trading days as Wall Street applauded the election results and bet that the Fed, the nation's central bank, would hold the line on interest rates amid signs that the economy was slowing and inflation was in check.

The central bank's policy-makers ended their meeting and left the key federal funds and discount rates unchanged. The funds rate, which commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans, remained at 5.25 percent and the discount rate, which the Fed charges banks for cash, stayed at 5 percent.

The goverment's latest statistics confirmed that inflation was not a problem. The Producer Price Index for October rose 0.4 percent, and the core rate, excluding the volatile food and energy components, fell 0.3 percent -- the sharpest drop since a 0.4 percent decline in October 1994.

"The near-term momentum can carry us higher," said David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers. "But historically after-election euphoria leads to a market that peaks between Thanksgiving and Christmas."
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond slipped 4/32, lifting its yield to 6.45 percent from Tuesday's eight-month low of 6.44 percent.

Meanwhile, gold prices closed higher following gains in mining stocks and technically motivated buying. Gold closed up 80 cents at $384.20 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange. December silver ended up 1.8 cents at $4.90 an ounce.

"It is interesting that gold stocks have been creeping up for the last few days for no reason with inflation under control," said Robert Stovall of Stovall/Twenty-First. Historically, the precious metal has risen in times of inflationary worries.

The dollar rose to 111.80 yen from 111.47 late on Tuesday, and to 1.5078 German marks from 1.5072. Meanwhile, the pound jumped more than one cent to $1.6597, its highest close since October 1992, from $1.6468 late on Tuesday.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil and product prices shot higher on the outlook for bitter cold weather this week in the Northeast.

Heating oil for December delivery settled up 2.95 cents at 71.20 cents a gallon, December unleaded gasoline up 2.57 cent a gallon at 68.34 cent a gallon and December crude oil up 77 cents at $24.12 a barrel.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat prices rose for a second straight day as export prospects brightened. December wheat closed 9-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $4.00-3/4.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 share index lost 7.4 points to 3,926.9. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 average had lost 226.99 points or 1.07 percent to 20,979.44.
